findings.text: Poverty shown, and poverty real, are not the same: one pretends to be rich, yet has nothing; another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth. Pretends is the reflexive of the verb for being rich and being poor (one makes himself rich, another makes himself poor), and the verification is in what he has, not in what he presents (Prov 13:7). Prov 13:8 then gives poverty a side of its own: the poor man hears no threat.

findings.text: Blessed are the poor in spirit (Matt 5:3) locates the poverty in spirit, not in means: poverty placed in the spirit, with those who mourn following (Matt 5:4).

In Psalm 109:21-26 poor and needy is said of himself by the one who prays. It is joined at once to the heart (my heart is stricken) and the body (gaunt), and it ends in an appeal, Help me: needy as an appeal for help, made to God.

In Psalm 34:4-6 and 69:29-33 the poor man cries, and is heard: this poor man cried, and the Lord heard him and saved him out of all his troubles (34:4, 6); I am afflicted and in pain, the Lord hears the needy (69:29, 33). The poor man is the one who speaks, and his fear is among what he is delivered from (34:4).

Nathan's parable (2 Sam 12:3-4) gives the poor man's side as attachment to the little he has: the poor man had nothing but one little ewe lamb, which was like a daughter to him, against the rich man who was unwilling to take one of his own flock.
Exodus 30:15: rich and poor give the same half shekel, to make atonement for your lives.
On the researcher's three dimensions of poverty, the verses corroborate the first, poor as means (lacking external resources, wealth): Exo 30:15 and 2 Sam 12:3.
On the researcher's three dimensions of poverty, the verses corroborate the second, poor as an inner state, which may not match the means: Mat 5:3 and Pro 13:7.
On the researcher's three dimensions of poverty, the verses corroborate the third, needy as an appeal: Psa 109:22-26 and 34:6. Nothing found sets the three dimensions against each other.
